photo.name: photographic print; album
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); album
photo.reason: Studio portrait of Struck by the Ree, a Yankton-Yanktonai Dakota chief, wearing traditional fur hat with eagle feather, shirt, fur blanket, embroidered leggings and moccasins, holding a pipe-tomahawk — a clear documentary photo of Dakota dress and regalia.

photo.name: photographic print; album
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); album
photo.reason: This is a studio portrait of named Brulé (Sicangu) Lakota/Sioux chiefs and women in traditional dress with dentalium ornaments, feather bonnet, pipe, and blanket; Lakota is a closely related division of the Sioux alongside Dakota, so the image is acceptable evidence of the broader Sioux cultural group's dress and regalia even if the museum label specifies the Lakota (not Dakota) branch.

photo.name: photographic print; album
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); album
photo.reason: Studio portrait of Wicked Bear, a Brulé Sioux chief, shown wearing authentic dress (eagle feather, dentalium/abalone ear ornaments, bone breastplate, cloth shirt/vest, blanket); Brulé are part of the wider Sioux/Dakota-Lakota nation, so this documentary photo of traditional dress fits the claimed ethnicity.

photo.name: photographic print; album
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); album
photo.reason: Studio portrait of Two Lances, a Yankton-Yanktonai chief (Yankton and Yanktonai are Dakota divisions), shown in full traditional regalia—eagle feathers, quilled/beaded war shirt, leggings, moccasins, tomahawk and bag—clearly documenting Dakota dress and material culture.

photo.name: photographic print; album
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); album
photo.reason: Studio portrait of Struck by the Ree, principal chief of the Yankton Sioux (Dakota/Nakota), seated in traditional dress with hairpipe/shell neck ornament, shirt, and blanket — a documentary photo of Dakota dress and a named Dakota leader.

photo.name: photographic print; album
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); album
photo.reason: Studio portrait of Cetannapewakan (Sacred Hand Hawk), identified as a Dakota Sioux man, wearing an eagle feather headdress, beaded shirt, and bandolier — documentary photo of Dakota dress and regalia.

photo.name: photographic print; album
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); album
photo.reason: Studio portrait of Smutty Bear, a Yankton-Yanktonai Dakota chief, wearing traditional embroidered/quilled warrior clothing, headdress feather, leggings, and moccasins, seated beside an interpreter in Western dress; this documentary photo clearly shows Dakota dress and material culture.

photo.name: photographic print; album
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); album
photo.reason: Studio portrait of Standing Soldier, a named Santee Dakota man, holding a pipe and pipe-bag, documenting Dakota dress and material culture even though photographed in Washington DC by an outside photographer.

photo.name: photographic print; glass negative
photo.title: photographic print (black and white); glass negative
photo.reason: The image shows a newspaper clipping photograph of Chief Yellow Thunder, identified as Yankton-Yanktonai, a Dakota/Sioux subgroup, wearing a feathered warbonnet and decorated shirt — this documents traditional Dakota dress and regalia.

painting-mss.name: Wintercount, fotografi, photograph
painting-mss.title: Wintercount, fotografi, photograph
painting-mss.reason: A painted buffalo-hide winter count, a pictographic record-keeping tradition practiced by the Lakota/Dakota (Oceti Sakowin) people, shown with its symbolic annual markers. This is a genuine Dakota/Sioux cultural artifact.

painting-mss.name: oil painting
painting-mss.title: oil painting
painting-mss.reason: Portrait of Yellow Hawk, a Dakota (Sans Arc Lakota) chief, in full regalia with feather headdress, ornaments, decorated shirt, and pipe-tomahawk — painted by an outsider artist but depicting documented Dakota dress and material culture.

household.name: knivslida, fodral, knife sheath [[Etno]], case [[Etno]], étui de couteau
household.title: knivslida, fodral, knife sheath [[Etno]], case [[Etno]], étui de couteau
household.reason: A hide knife sheath with quilled geometric decoration (porcupine-quill mosaic), attributed to Dakota in the museum's catalogue notes; this matches known Plains/Dakota quillwork traditions.

household.name: scraper
household.title: scraper
household.reason: The image shows a bone scraper/tool with a worked handle and toothed edge, a traditional household implement attributed to the Dakota; this is a plausible utilitarian object type for the culture.

arms.name: Piptomahawk, photography, Piph
arms.title: Piptomahawk, photography, Piph
arms.reason: Two pipe-tomahawks with metal blades and long wooden handles, a classic Plains Sioux (Dakota/Oceti Sakowin) form combining weapon and pipe, matching the museum's Sioux attribution.

arms.name: spear-head
arms.title: spear-head
arms.reason: A flaked stone spear-point, a projectile weapon type plausible for Dakota material culture, consistent with the museum's attribution.

garment.name: cap
garment.title: cap
garment.reason: A fully beaded cloth cap in military-cap shape with Northern Plains-style lazy-stitch beadwork, geometric stars, and US flag motifs — a well-documented Dakota/Lakota beadwork form (patriotic militia-style caps) attributed here to Dakota makers.

garment.name: huvudbonad, fjäderskrud, headgear
garment.title: huvudbonad, fjäderskrud, headgear
garment.reason: This is a feather headdress ("roach"/warbonnet-style) with beaded diadem band and trailing ribbons, described explicitly as being like Dakota chiefs' feather regalia — a classic Plains Sioux/Dakota garment form, with characteristic geometric beadwork (stars, boxes) typical of Plains beadwork traditions.

masks-ritual.name: amulett, Skinnpung., amulet
masks-ritual.title: amulett, Skinnpung., amulet
masks-ritual.reason: The image shows a beadwork lizard/turtle-form amulet, a well-documented Sioux (Oceti Sakowin/Lakota-Dakota) type used to hold an infant's umbilical cord, matching a known comparative example from the Teton Sioux cited in the museum's own correspondence.

jewelry.name: halsband, halsprydnad, krage, necklace, collier
jewelry.title: halsband, halsprydnad, krage, necklace, collier
jewelry.reason: This is a bear-claw necklace made of otter fur strip with bear claws, red cloth, and blue beads — a classic type of Plains chief's ornament, consistent with Dakota (Plains Sioux) material culture.

instruments.name: Frame Drum
instruments.title: Frame Drum
instruments.reason: A hide-covered frame drum with a painted bison and beater, attributed to the Teton Dakota (Lakota); such hand drums with animal motifs are typical of Plains peoples like the Dakota/Lakota.
